articleTitle: The 'step wise' planning approach to software projects
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Project Management for Software Engineers
abstract: There is a growing awareness of the importance of software project management (SPM) to which recognition of software engineering as a discipline has contributed. Evidence of this includes the publication of PRINCE, the government standards for the management of IT projects; the Certificate in Project Management that is administered by the Information Systems Examinations Board and the formation of PROMS-G, the BCS special interest group for project management. The University of Brighton has responded to this interest. The original focus was on the development of a module for the inter-university Modular Masters in Software Engineering (MMSE) which allows industrial practitioners to obtain an MSc by completing modules of their choice from a range offered by a number of different universities in the UK. A module would require the attendance at a intensive course for a week, these courses being also open to others not participating in the overall scheme. The SPM material developed has subsequently been used in customised forms on a range of other courses, both undergraduate and post-graduate.

articleTitle: Enhanced software project management by application of metrics and cost estimation techniques
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Project Management for Software Engineers
abstract: This paper describes elements of an improvement project within a collaborative partnership between the University of Cambridge and GPT Ltd, the UK's largest supplier of telecommunications solutions. The project aims to identify, formulate and collect a series of key measures to aid project planning and control through the provision of valid quantitative project data, and to stimulate software process improvement. In the paper the approach to metrics implementation is discussed and recently developed cost estimation techniques are introduced.

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Project Management for Software Engineers
abstract: Many projects fail because when things start going wrong they cannot easily be rectified, and the problems are compounded because the right people are not available or involved in the project and the right systems are not in place. Only by creating a project infrastructure at the initiation stage of the project can this hazard be minimised or avoided. The paper discusses the issues involved and presents the important aspects of a project infrastructure.

articleTitle: Project management in rapid application development
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Project Management for Software Engineers
abstract: This work deals with some of the principles upon which rapid application development (RAD) projects are managed, based on recent case studies and published methods. It focuses particularly on the development team, and suggests themes that may underlie RAD principles. An approach to metrics in establishing the relationship between principles and benefits is discussed.

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Project Management for Software Engineers
abstract: We were invited to audit a project for a client. This project had missed its final delivery date, had overshot it's budget and also failed to meet performance criteria in a number of key areas. Further, some software remained to be produced. These problems were due to lack of adequate project management infrastructure and this paper describes those techniques of project management which would have prevented these problems arising, and further how they contributed to a swift turnaround in the project once properly applied.

articleTitle: A proposed curriculum for software engineering project management process, product and people
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Project Management for Software Engineers
abstract: We propose a curriculum for software engineering project management. For each major topic, we identify useful starting points for study, plus relevant resources and standards, including resources available electronically. We adapt Bush and Fenton's (1990) classification of the software engineering domain whereby we can describe all entities to be managed in a software project as being either process, product, or people. This provides a useful framework for consideration of software project management topics. The curriculum is presented according to the following format: area (process, product, people), major topic, sub-topic, priority (essential, desirable, optional), relevant resources.
